chapters.title: Book IX
chapters.hook: An empty sleeve in the consent binder asks Nathan for truth before anyone asks who failed.
chapters.counterintuition: Anger can look like justice when a lie hurts people. Instead, let truth correct the shared world without adding fever to the injury.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before correcting someone, write the truthful action needed and the anger you must not add to it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat lies and injustice as damage to shared reality: correct what can be corrected, speak plainly, and refuse the anger that would make you another wrongdoer.

breakdown.fastRead:
The consent binder has a clean empty sleeve where page six should be. Nathan can protect the lab image by enrolling one more patient and finding blame later, or he can stop enrollment and send the audit email now. The missing page is not only paperwork. It is trust removed from the room.

Truth is not a private preference here. It is the condition that lets rational creatures share a world.

Justice begins by refusing to lie about the fact in front of you.
breakdown.deepRead:
Truth is not a private preference here; it is the condition that lets rational creatures share a world. A lie breaks more than a rule. It asks other people to live inside a false map. Injustice does the same by treating rational beings as material for private advantage.

That is why anger is an unreliable servant. It may notice the wrong quickly, but it also wants display, punishment, and heat. Chloe can show copied essays without humiliating the student. Nathan can stop enrollment before naming a culprit. Rebecca can photograph the prep fridge before staged trays replace the real condition.

Mildness is active strength, not weakness.

It is a method for keeping the fact clean. When heat enters first, the correction starts collecting extra material: guesses about motive, pleasure in exposure, a wish to make the wrongdoer smaller. The fact needs less company than anger wants to give it.

The hard task is to keep correction clean. If someone lies, tell the truth. If a process hides risk, expose the risk. If a rumor is turning a family into suspects, remove the name from the flyer. None of that requires rage as fuel.

The limit is not softness toward wrongdoing. Some wrongs need formal consequences. The point is that correction should not become another wrong by adding contempt, exaggeration, or public theater where truth would have been enough.
breakdown.fullRead:
Wrongdoing is treated as a break with shared nature because rational creatures are made for one another. Lying is especially grave because it fights the very condition that lets people coordinate: truth. If the map is false, everyone who trusts it walks worse. The consent binder, the repair estimate, the temperature log, the copied code, the printed flyer: each is a small public world. Falsify it, and other people must live in the distortion.

What does anger add after the truth is already clear?

Sometimes it adds courage. More often, it adds heat that wants to be mistaken for courage. Nathan does not need rage to stop enrollment. He needs the consent binder, the enrollment log, and the audit email. Chloe does not need humiliation to address plagiarism. She needs the printed essays, the similarity report, and a meeting where the truth is spoken without spectacle.

The phrase universal nature named truth makes lying more than personal preference. The liar damages relation itself. The unjust person does wrong against the other person and also against himself because he makes his own ruling faculty worse. That is a severe claim: every unjust action deforms the actor too.

Rebecca's food safety inspection shows the point without drama. The prep fridge smells faintly sour behind a new parsley garnish. A manager is replacing real trays before the inspector arrives. Rebecca photographs the fridge and temperature log before the staged version appears. She is not hunting for a public win. She is preserving the true condition customers depend on.

The Cicero note reinforces the pressure: justice is not an attitude kept clean in storage. Virtue belongs in action. That action may be a report, a correction, a refusal, a private issue with exact diff links, or a public timeline that removes a family's name from a rumor. The form varies. The standard does not.

Akira's open-source dispute is a useful edge case. A contributor copied code without attribution. Public shaming would feel righteous and might also become its own injustice. Akira opens a private issue first, includes exact diff links, points to the license file, and gives a repair path before any accusation is posted. Truth stays sharp. The fever stays out.

A correction can be severe without becoming theatrical. The missing consent form can stop enrollment. The unsafe prep tray can be photographed. The false flyer can be pulled. Each act protects the shared world more effectively when it does not ask rage to certify its seriousness.

Mildness has to remain active. It is not the mildness of looking away, and it is not the mildness of pleasing everyone. It is the strength to correct without needing anger to prove sincerity. Wipe out imagination. Check the appetite for revenge. Put present conduct toward social good. Tell the truth in the form that can repair the shared world.

examples.title: Nathan Stops Enrollment

planSpec.audience: Nathan discovering a missing consent form
planSpec.stakes: concealment would protect the lab image and injure trust
planSpec.requiredBeat: Nathan stops enrollment for the day and reports the missing consent before discussing blame.

examples.scenario: The consent binder has a clean empty sleeve where page six should be, and Nathan sees the enrollment log already prepared for the afternoon. The audit email is open in a draft window. One more participant would keep the lab on pace, but the missing form has made the next honest action visible. The clinic hallway is full, and the next signature line will affect a real participant.
examples.whatToDo: Stop enrollment for the day, report the missing consent in the audit email, and discuss blame only after the truth is recorded.
examples.whyItMatters: Concealment would protect the lab image by injuring shared trust. Nathan keeps justice clean by correcting the fact before hunting for a culprit.

examples.title: Chloe Shows the Matching Paragraphs

planSpec.audience: Chloe confronting copied essays
planSpec.stakes: anger could make correction feel like humiliation
planSpec.requiredBeat: "We are going to tell the truth without making a spectacle," Chloe says before showing the matching paragraphs.

examples.scenario: Chloe says, "The evidence is enough," at the conference table. The printed essays sit beside the similarity report, with three matching paragraphs highlighted. The student is staring at the table edge. Chloe's next sentence can humiliate him or show the copied passages and the repair path without spectacle. The essays sit side by side on the desk, with the similarity report clipped to the folder.
examples.whatToDo: Show the matching paragraphs, name the plagiarism plainly, and explain the repair consequence without turning the meeting into a public shaming.
examples.whyItMatters: Truth does not need humiliation to become clear. Chloe corrects the wrong while refusing to add a second injury for the sake of anger.

examples.title: Mateusz Reads the Full Estimate

planSpec.audience: Mateusz hearing a board member hide repair costs
planSpec.stakes: truth affects every resident's future fees
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 7:03 p.m., Mateusz asks the treasurer to read the full repair estimate into the minutes.

examples.scenario: At 7:03 in the evening, Mateusz sees the treasurer fold the repair estimate under her notebook while the reserve fund sheet passes down the table. Mateusz sees the meeting minutes still open. Residents will vote on fees next month, and the hidden number changes every future bill. He asks for the full estimate to be read aloud. The reserve spreadsheet is projected in the room, and every future fee depends on the number.
examples.whatToDo: Ask the treasurer to read the full repair estimate into the minutes and attach it to the reserve fund sheet before any vote proceeds.
examples.whyItMatters: The cost is not private board discomfort. It belongs to residents' future fees, so the shared record has to carry the whole truth.

examples.title: Rebecca Photographs the Fridge

planSpec.audience: Rebecca watching a manager stage-clean for the inspector
planSpec.stakes: false appearance could put customers at risk
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rebecca photographs the prep fridge before the staged trays replace the real ones.

examples.scenario: The prep fridge smells faintly sour behind the new parsley garnish. Rebecca remembers the manager reaching for staged trays while the temperature log sat unsigned. In her report, the decisive moment is the camera roll: she photographed the real fridge before the cleaner version replaced it. The thermometer is still on the shelf when the garnish tray slides into view.
examples.whatToDo: Photograph the prep fridge, record the unsigned temperature log, and preserve the real condition before the staged trays hide it.
examples.whyItMatters: A staged appearance would make customers live inside a false safety picture. Rebecca's evidence protects the truth before it can be dressed up.

examples.title: Akira Opens the Private Issue

planSpec.audience: Akira handling a contributor who copied code without attribution
planSpec.stakes: public shaming might become another form of injustice
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Akira open a private issue with exact diff links and a repair path before posting any accusation.

examples.scenario: Akira sees the copied function line up in two browser panes, with the license file open behind the diff links. Akira has a draft public post ready, sharp enough to win the room. Instead, he opens a private issue first, lists the exact lines, and gives the contributor a repair path before any accusation goes public. The license file is open in one pane and the copied function is highlighted in another.
examples.whatToDo: Open the private issue, include exact diff links and the license file, and offer a repair path before making a public accusation.
examples.whyItMatters: The copying needs correction, but public shaming can become another injustice. Akira keeps truth exact and gives repair a chance before heat takes over.

examples.title: Lea Removes the Family Name

planSpec.audience: Lea correcting false rumors after a break-in
planSpec.stakes: fear is turning one family into suspects without evidence
planSpec.requiredBeat: How do you defend safety without feeding a lie?

examples.scenario: Lea asks, "How do you defend safety without feeding a lie?" Lea stands between community hall chairs with the police timeline in one hand and a printed flyer in the other. A family's name appears under suspicious activity with no evidence beside it. She reads the timeline aloud, crosses out the name, and rewrites the warning around confirmed facts. The flyer draft is one click from print, and the family has not been contacted. The flyer stack is still warm from the printer.
examples.whatToDo: Read the police timeline aloud, remove the family's name from the flyer, and replace suspicion with confirmed safety information.
examples.whyItMatters: Fear wants a target, but a false target injures the shared world. Lea protects safety by refusing to let rumor borrow the voice of truth.

questions.prompt: A lab discovers a missing consent form and wants to keep enrolling until someone can explain the mistake. What is the first just act? The waiting room is active, and every new signature would rest on a false record.
choices: Find who misplaced the page before taking action.
Enroll only low-risk participants until the file is fixed.
Stop enrollment and report the missing consent.
questions.explanation: Truth has to enter the record before blame. Continuing enrollment asks participants and staff to live inside a false picture of consent.

questions.prompt: A teacher has proof of copied essays and feels angry enough to make the meeting painful. What should guide the correction? The student is already outside the office, and the printed proof is on the desk.
choices: Make the student feel the seriousness through public shame.
Show the evidence plainly and set a repair consequence without spectacle.
Avoid direct language so the student does not feel attacked.
questions.explanation: The wrong needs truth and consequence, not humiliation or vagueness. Public shame adds heat that can become its own injustice.

questions.prompt: A co-op board hides the full repair estimate while discussing future fees. What response fits shared truth? The meeting packet will go to residents tonight, so the hidden number will shape real choices.
choices: Wait for the treasurer to disclose it voluntarily.
Privately warn residents after the meeting.
Ask for the full estimate to be read into the minutes.
questions.explanation: The fees affect everyone, so the shared record needs the whole number. Private warning leaves the formal decision inside a partial truth.

questions.prompt: When a restaurant manager starts replacing unsafe prep trays before inspection. What should Rebecca preserve first? The inspector is ten minutes away, and the staged tray would erase the fact customers need.
choices: The manager's motive for staging the trays.
The inspector's likely reaction.
The real prep fridge condition and temperature log.
questions.explanation: The true condition is the fact customers depend on. Motive and reaction may matter later, but the first duty is to preserve reality before staging replaces it.

questions.prompt: The open-source maintainer finds copied code and can win public support by shaming the contributor. What is the cleaner first move? The repository is public, but the repair path can still be precise before it becomes spectacle.
choices: Post publicly so others learn not to copy code.
Ignore it if the copied code improves the project.
Open a private issue with exact diff links and a repair path.
questions.explanation: The copying needs correction, but exact private repair keeps truth sharp without adding needless public injury. Ignoring it abandons attribution.

questions.prompt: During a case where safety committee wants to leave an unverified family name on a flyer after a break-in. What is the moral risk? The printer tray is loaded, and the wrong name would travel faster than correction.
choices: Fear can turn a falsehood into public injury.
Flyers are ineffective during public fear.
The committee may look less decisive.
questions.explanation: The unverified name gives fear a target and damages shared truth. Effectiveness and image are secondary to the false accusation.

questions.prompt: In a situation where manager says anger proves she cares about justice. What distinction should she make? The team is watching her face, and the next sentence can be fact or fever.
choices: Care is proven by truthful correction, not by the heat added to it.
Anger should be hidden so others do not object.
Justice works best when people fear consequences.
questions.explanation: Anger may notice wrong, but it does not prove justice. The test is whether truth and correction happen without added contempt or exaggeration.

questions.prompt: After a scenario where false report helps one department avoid embarrassment but causes others to make bad plans. Why is the lie worse than private dishonesty? The false report will become the map for teams that never saw the embarrassment.
choices: It damages the shared map other people use to act.
It makes the department look unprofessional if discovered.
It creates more paperwork when corrected.
questions.explanation: A lie injures common reality. Reputation and paperwork are smaller effects; the deeper harm is that others act inside a false map.

questions.prompt: Two corrections are possible. One is accurate but humiliating; the other is accurate, firm, and gives a repair path. Which is stronger? The repair meeting is private, but the consequences will become public if truth is bent.
choices: The humiliating one, because pain helps wrongdoers remember.
The firm repair path, because truth stays active without adding a second injury.
Neither, because wrongdoing should be left alone when anger is present.
questions.explanation: The second option keeps truth and correction while refusing private fever. Leaving wrongdoing alone fails justice, and humiliation confuses heat with strength.

reviewCards.front: What should come before blame when a serious record is false or incomplete?
reviewCards.back: Stop the affected action and put the truth into the record. Blame can wait until shared reality is restored.

reviewCards.front: Why is lying more than private dishonesty?
reviewCards.back: A lie damages the shared map other people use to act. It makes rational cooperation happen inside false conditions.

reviewCards.front: How can anger corrupt correction?
reviewCards.back: It can add humiliation, exaggeration, revenge, or public theater. Truth needs firmness, not private fever.

reviewCards.front: What does mildness mean when someone has done wrong?
reviewCards.back: It means correcting without becoming another wrongdoer. Mildness can report, stop, refuse, or impose consequences without hatred steering the act.

reviewCards.front: Why does justice belong in action?
reviewCards.back: An attitude toward truth is not enough. Justice has to enter the record, the meeting, the report, the issue, or the flyer where shared life is being distorted.

implementationPlan.title: Correcting Without the Fever of Anger
implementationPlan.coreSkill: You practice separating truthful correction from the anger that wants to ride with it. The skill is to record the truth, choose the repair path, and leave out contempt.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a consent or safety record is missing, then stop the affected action and report the fact before discussing blame.
If a student has copied work, then show the evidence and consequence without turning the meeting into humiliation.
If fear names a suspect without evidence, then remove the name and replace it with confirmed facts.
If attribution is violated, then open a precise repair path before making a public accusation.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before one correction today, write the truthful action needed and the anger you must not add. Then make the correction in that order.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Review one conflict each week. Separate the fact, the repair, the consequence, and the heat you added. Rewrite the next response with the heat removed.

memorableLines.text: Justice begins by refusing to lie about the fact in front of you.
memorableLines.why: It makes justice concrete before blame starts.

memorableLines.text: Mildness is active strength, not weakness.
memorableLines.why: The short line protects firmness from becoming rage.

memorableLines.text: What does anger add after the truth is already clear?
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a direct diagnostic question for righteous anger.

chapters.title: Book X
chapters.hook: Snow presses the clinic windows, and Simon has to decide whether careful still means careful here.
chapters.counterintuition: Treating a character name as affirmation makes it fragile. Instead, use it as a standard that must survive the conditions trying to rename you.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one name of character you claim, then identify the condition that most often makes you drop it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Hold a few names like true, modest, rational, and careful without needing others to call you that; conditions test the name, but they do not get to rewrite it.

breakdown.fastRead:
Snow presses against the clinic windows before the first chart opens. Simon wants a better posting, a larger staff, a city hospital, a life where careful work feels recognized. Instead, he writes careful at the top of the patient board and handles the next chart as if this place were permanent.

A name of character is not proven by saying it. It is proven when the condition that usually weakens it arrives and the name still governs the act.

Do not wait for a cleaner life to be clean.
breakdown.deepRead:
The few names matter because conditions keep trying to rename you. Good, modest, true, rational, steady, magnanimous: these are not labels for self-esteem. They are assignments. If you lose them, return quickly. If you keep them only when others approve, you never possessed them deeply.

Plato enters as a reminder that a narrow place does not require a narrow soul. A person can live inside city walls, a clinic rotation, a production floor, a cramped newsroom, or a review desk and still range over human things with a larger mind.

The wounded arena fighter is the image of a life that keeps choosing the same claws.

The old comparison to the Bestiarii is brutal. A half-devoured fighter begs to be kept for tomorrow, only to face the same teeth again. That is what it looks like to keep returning to conditions that tear away your names while asking for one more day of the same life.

The limit is that names are not slogans. Julia rejects the sample jacket because true quality cannot depend on whether the defect stays hidden. Patrick puts the correction above the fold online because honest does not wait for social reaction.

A name becomes real at the point of friction. Careful meets the chart no one will audit. True meets the defect hidden inside the sample cuff. Fair meets the room that applauds the wrong evidence. Without that meeting, the name is only decoration.
breakdown.fullRead:
A soul is asked to become good, simple, one, and naked: not bare in the theatrical sense, but free of the costumes that make character depend on setting. Better weather, better company, a nicer posting, a more appreciative audience, a cleaner body, a smoother reputation: all of these can become conditions you demand before you agree to be what you claim.

Which condition most often changes your name?

For Simon, it is location. The remote clinic gives him a reason to call thin care temporary. For Julia, it is speed and style pressure on a fashion production floor. For Patrick, it is embarrassment at the correction desk. For Nora, it is praise from a developer. For Matthew, applause in a debate room. For Anke, pride before client pickup.

Zeno's definition keeps the scale larger than personal comfort. The perfect living being, the good and just whole, is not arranged around your preferred climate, society, or reputation. That wider scale is meant to loosen the demand that life first become pleasing before you become steady.

Plato's image of dwelling within city walls while the mind ranges beyond them helps here too. A narrow assignment does not require a narrow character. The clinic is small. The patient board is still a place for careful. The flood map may cover a glossy rendering. Rational still has work to do.

Bestiarii could be torn by beasts in public, and the old warning still cuts in quieter rooms: do not be torn by names, praise, weather, and appetite before anyone else touches you. Keep the inner animal from taking orders from the outer noise.

The names must also be held without needing to be called by them. If you need the room to call you fair, you will bend toward applause. Matthew sees it after a debate round. The confident speaker gets the room, but the evidence cards do not support half the claims. He lowers the speaker score after checking his notes, not because he wants to look severe, but because fair has to survive applause.

There is a hard mercy in quick return. If you lose the name, return to it. Do not build an identity around the lapse. Do not beg the same claws to keep you for another day. Move to the place, task, or act where the name can be maintained again.

A name also has to survive the body's plea for relief. Hunger, soreness, weather, and fatigue all ask to be treated as exceptions, but the standard is meant to govern exactly when the exception feels plausible.

Anke runs one thumbnail across a crack in a walnut table before delivery. Pride wants the sale, the wax cloth is ready, and the delivery straps are on the bench. The name on the invoice is hers. She delays pickup and repairs the crack. That is what a character name does when it is more than sound: it interrupts the sale that would make the name false.

examples.title: Simon Writes Careful

planSpec.audience: Simon wanting a better posting before he acts well
planSpec.stakes: location becomes his excuse for thin care
planSpec.requiredBeat: Simon writes "careful" on the top of the patient board and handles the next chart as if the posting were permanent.

examples.scenario: Snow presses against the clinic windows before the first chart opens, and Simon's parka hangs beside the satellite phone. He has been calling the rotation temporary for three weeks. On the patient board, above the day's names, he writes careful, then opens the next chart as if the posting were permanent. The waiting room list is short, but the next chart still belongs to someone who will not know he felt temporary.
examples.whatToDo: Write careful on the patient board, take the next chart seriously, and let the name govern the work instead of the posting.
examples.whyItMatters: Location has been renaming Simon's standards. The board makes the claimed character name answer to the patient in front of him.

examples.title: Julia Rejects the Hidden Defect

planSpec.audience: Julia measuring a rushed sample
planSpec.stakes: style pressure could rename dishonesty as speed
planSpec.requiredBeat: Julia rejects the sample under her own quality name before anyone else sees the defect.

examples.scenario: Loose black thread curls from the jacket cuff while Julia lays the measuring tape across the rushed sample. The quality tag is already printed, and the showroom team wants speed. The defect is small enough to hide in motion, but the sample will carry her signoff. She marks reject before anyone else sees the cuff. The showroom rack is ready, and the loose thread is asking whether true quality can survive pressure.
examples.whatToDo: Reject the sample, note the cuff defect on the quality tag, and let her name mean the same thing before and after anyone notices.
examples.whyItMatters: Speed is trying to rename dishonesty as practicality. Julia keeps the quality name real by refusing a hidden defect while it is still easy to pass.

examples.title: Patrick Places the Correction High

planSpec.audience: Patrick deciding whether to bury a correction
planSpec.stakes: public embarrassment tests the name true
planSpec.requiredBeat: "Put the correction above the fold online," Patrick says, before checking social reaction.

examples.scenario: "Put the correction where readers will see it," Patrick says, with the correction note open in the CMS draft and the analytics screen already showing the original story's traffic. Burying it would be easy. His hand is near refresh, but true has to speak before social reaction gets a vote. The homepage slot is still open, so honest has to appear where the first error traveled.
examples.whatToDo: Publish the correction high on the story page before checking reactions, and let the correction note match the size of the error.
examples.whyItMatters: Public embarrassment tests whether true is a working name or only a private preference. Patrick keeps the name by correcting where readers were misled.

examples.title: Nora Covers the Rendering

planSpec.audience: Nora facing a developer's praise
planSpec.stakes: flattery could pull her from modest and rational into approval-seeking
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Nora compare the plan to the flood map, not to the compliment she just received.

examples.scenario: You see the flood map cover the glossy rendering while Nora keeps one finger on the zoning table. The developer has just praised her practical judgment in front of the room. She nods once, then compares the drainage plan to the flood line instead of to the compliment still hanging in the air. The developer keeps smiling at the rendering, and the flood line quietly asks which name Nora will keep.
examples.whatToDo: Put the flood map over the rendering, check the zoning table, and let the plan answer to water and law, not praise.
examples.whyItMatters: Flattery tries to rename approval-seeking as judgment. Nora stays rational by making the physical map outrank the compliment.

examples.title: Matthew Lowers the Applauded Score

planSpec.audience: Matthew tempted to reward confidence over truth
planSpec.stakes: the room's applause pressures the score sheet
planSpec.requiredBeat: Which name survives the applause: fair, or impressed?

examples.scenario: Which name survives the applause: fair, or impressed? Matthew looks at the score sheet after the timer light goes dark. The winning speaker had the room, but the evidence cards do not support two central claims. In his postmortem notes, he lowers the speaker score after checking each unsupported line. The trophy table is being reset behind him, and the evidence cards are less charming than the applause.
examples.whatToDo: Check the evidence cards against the claims, lower the speaker score, and let fair survive the room's applause.
examples.whyItMatters: Confidence can make impressed feel like fair. Matthew protects the judging name by returning to evidence after the room has already chosen its favorite.

examples.title: Anke Delays the Walnut Table

planSpec.audience: Anke finding a small crack before client pickup
planSpec.stakes: pride wants the sale, character wants the repair
planSpec.requiredBeat: It took Anke one thumbnail across the crack to know the table was not ready to carry her name.

examples.scenario: It took Anke one thumbnail to hear the crack catch. The walnut table glowed under the wax cloth, and the delivery straps were already laid out for client pickup. Pride wanted the sale to go through. The catch under her nail told her the table was not ready to carry her name. The client pickup text is already sent, which makes the repair a test of craft instead of mood.
examples.whatToDo: Delay pickup, mark the crack, and repair the walnut table before letting her name travel with it.
examples.whyItMatters: The crack is small, but the name is not. Anke keeps character from becoming branding by stopping the sale that would make her standard false.

questions.prompt: A clinician says he is careful but treats a remote posting as a place where thin work is acceptable. What should he test? The satellite phone is silent, and no supervisor will see the next chart.
choices: Whether the posting deserves his best effort.
Whether other clinicians are also cutting corners.
Whether careful still governs the next chart in this location.
questions.explanation: The name must survive the condition. Asking whether the posting deserves care lets location rename him, and comparing others avoids the present chart.

questions.prompt: A production lead can hide a tiny defect in a rushed sample. What action keeps her quality name real? The showroom team is waiting, and the hidden cuff thread will not stay hidden forever.
choices: Ship it because the defect is unlikely to be noticed.
Ask the showroom team whether speed matters more this week.
Reject the sample and mark the defect before anyone else sees it.
questions.explanation: The hidden defect tests the name precisely because nobody else sees it yet. Asking about speed hands character to pressure.

questions.prompt: A local editor has to correct a widely read error. What should true mean in this setting? The original error is still getting traffic, so placement matters more than embarrassment.
choices: Post the correction quietly to avoid distracting from current news.
Wait to see if readers notice the original mistake.
Publish the correction where affected readers will see it.
questions.explanation: True has to match the reach of the error. Quiet posting or waiting protects embarrassment while leaving readers misled.

questions.prompt: The planner receives flattering praise from a developer before reviewing flood risk. Which move keeps rational judgment intact? The flood map and zoning table are both on the table while the developer praises her.
choices: Thank the developer and give the rendering extra attention.
Set the flood map over the rendering and check the zoning table.
Ignore all developer comments as manipulation.
questions.explanation: The flood map and zoning table return judgment to the object. Praise may be sincere, but it cannot become the standard of review.

questions.prompt: During a case where debate judge is impressed by a confident speaker whose evidence cards do not support key claims. What should fair require? The debate room is loud, but the evidence cards are still the standard.
choices: Reward confidence because persuasion is part of debate.
Lower the score after checking unsupported claims.
Split the difference so the room's response is partly honored.
questions.explanation: Fair cannot be renamed by applause. Confidence matters only within the rules of evidence, so unsupported claims must affect the score.

questions.prompt: In a situation where craftsperson finds a small crack before delivery and knows the client may never notice. Why delay the sale? The delivery straps are laid out, and the crack catches under her thumbnail.
choices: Because every flaw makes a product unusable.
Pride can pull attention toward comparison with other makers, distracting from the standard inside this table.
Because the product will carry her name whether or not the client sees the flaw.
questions.explanation: The crack tests the maker's standard, not only the client's eye. Some flaws may be minor, but a hidden one still asks whether her name means anything.

questions.prompt: Someone repeats, I am honest, modest, and rational, but changes behavior whenever praise or inconvenience arrives. What is the problem? The names sound noble until a condition tries to buy an exception.
choices: The names are labels, not standards under conditions.
The person has chosen too many names at once.
The names should be kept private to avoid pressure.
questions.explanation: A character name is tested by conditions. Quantity and privacy are secondary; the core failure is that the names do not govern action.

questions.prompt: After a scenario where worker waits for a better team, better office, and better mood before acting well. Which image corrects that excuse? The room is ready to reward him, but the card in his hand says otherwise.
choices: A narrow place does not require a narrow soul.
Better-ordered places shape cues and routines, so moving environments can improve conduct with less strain.
A difficult place proves the work is not suited to him.
questions.explanation: The Plato-inflected reminder is that condition does not get to shrink character. Better settings may help, but they cannot be required before goodness begins.

questions.prompt: Two people lose their character names under pressure. One builds a story around the lapse. The other returns quickly to the name in the next act. Who is closer?
choices: The second, because quick return keeps the name from becoming mere memory.
The first, because serious self-criticism prevents future failure.
Neither, because losing the name once proves it was false.
questions.explanation: The source pressure allows return. Self-drama can become another claw, while one lapse does not end the work if the next act restores the standard.

reviewCards.front: What turns a character name from affirmation into practice?
reviewCards.back: It governs an act under the condition that usually weakens it. Careful, true, fair, or rational has to survive the place, praise, body, or audience.

reviewCards.front: Why does a narrow place not excuse narrow conduct?
reviewCards.back: Your setting may be small, unpleasant, or temporary, but the next act can still be careful, true, fair, or rational.

reviewCards.front: What do the Bestiarii warn against?
reviewCards.back: A life that keeps choosing the same claws: returning to conditions or habits that tear away your names while asking for one more day unchanged.

reviewCards.front: How does praise threaten a character name?
reviewCards.back: Praise can rename approval-seeking as judgment. The antidote is to return to the object: map, evidence, defect, chart, or correction.

reviewCards.front: What should you do after losing a name like fair or true?
reviewCards.back: Return quickly in the next act. Do not build a self-punishing identity around the lapse; make the name govern again.

implementationPlan.title: Keeping the Name That Conduct Earns
implementationPlan.coreSkill: You practice treating character words as standards, not self-descriptions. The skill is to identify the condition that usually changes your conduct and make the next act answer to the name anyway.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a posting or shift feels temporary, then write the character name you need and apply it to the next chart or case.
If a hidden defect appears, then decide as if your name will be attached to the work forever.
If a correction embarrasses you, then place it where the original error did its damage.
If applause or praise pulls at you, then return to evidence before recording judgment.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one character name you claim. Identify the condition that most often weakens it, then make one act today that keeps the name under that condition.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one name you want to keep. List the condition that tested it, the act you chose, and the next quicker return if you lost it.

memorableLines.text: Do not wait for a cleaner life to be clean.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the condition-independent standard into a memorable sentence.

chapters.title: Book XI
chapters.hook: The triage printer jams while a furious hand hits the counter, and Fiona still has one useful act to finish.
chapters.counterintuition: Anger is not proof that you care about justice, but a force that can cut you from the people and task justice still needs.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do the next social act cleanly: correct what you can, keep benevolence intact, and refuse the anger that severs you from the whole.

breakdown.fastRead:
The triage printer jams, a family member shouts, and Fiona can feel the room pulling her toward a matching voice. The useful act is smaller and harder: name the wait, check the chart, give the next true update, and stay connected enough to keep serving the room.

Anger often disguises itself as moral energy. The test is whether it helps you complete the general-interest act. If it makes you louder, crueler, or eager to win, it has cut the branch from the tree. A corrected person should still be treated as kin. Mildness is not surrender when it keeps the work whole.
breakdown.deepRead:
Luca reads the code review twice. The comment is rude, the null fixture is real, and his first answer would be a clean little revenge. He can spend ten minutes defending his competence, or he can patch the case and leave one plain note: the bug was valid, the tone was not.

That is the split this lesson keeps asking you to notice. The act may need firmness. It may need correction, a boundary, a refusal, or a consequence. What it does not need is the inward break where another person stops being part of the same human whole and becomes only an enemy to defeat.

Anger cuts the branch before the saw arrives.

Diogenes appears where plain speech is meant to cure pride, not entertain it. Old comedy could strip pretension because it served a corrective purpose; it did not merely give resentment a clever costume. That distinction matters when you are tempted to say the savage thing because it is true. A truth used to humiliate has already begun serving vanity. A truth used to repair can stay simple.

Phocion marks the difference between calm strength and calm performance. If the face is mild but the inner speech is counting points, the calm is only another tactic. Genuine benevolence can say no, correct the error, report the harm, or end the conversation. It does those things without needing the other person to be shamed first.

Socrates keeps reappearing as a model for not letting other people's noise own the soul. Public opinion, domestic embarrassment, and insult are all tested by the same question: will you let this person determine the quality of your own act? If not, finish the act. Do it for the common interest, not for applause from your anger.
breakdown.fullRead:
Margaux stands under a leaning maple while orange tape snaps against the fence. One neighbor wants the whole branch gone. The other wants a public apology before anyone touches the saw. Margaux opens the property survey, marks the line, and puts the arborist note beside it. First the diseased limb. Then the hurt pride.

The rational soul is not complete because nothing interrupts it. It is complete because it can make each interrupted act whole. A dance can be spoiled if the music stops. A just response can still be finished in one sentence, one signature, one chart check, one refusal to hate.

What makes anger so persuasive is that it often begins near something real. The family member in the waiting room is frightened. The reviewer was insulting. The neighbor is careless. The volunteer is vain. The sibling knows exactly which old sentence will sting. You do not have to pretend harm is harmless. You have to keep the harm from recruiting you into a second harm.

Sophocles is useful only if the stage trains you not to rage at the larger stage outside it. Tragedy shows people caught in forces larger than preference, and that lesson is wasted if you leave the theater ready to curse every hard event in your own life. The point is not theatrical sorrow. The point is scale.

The branch and tree image is severe because it names anger as self-injury. Someone else can obstruct you, insult you, or act foolishly. Hatred is the motion by which you cut yourself away from the social body. You may be right about the offense and still wrong about the severing.

You can test this in the next hard conversation. Can you name the fact without adding contempt? Can you correct the mistake without performing wounded superiority? Can you remember your own errors before deciding that another person's error makes them alien? These questions do not make you soft. They keep your strength pointed at the work.

Mina sees the vanity in the charity kitchen. A volunteer keeps drifting toward the camera, overfilling plates when donors pass, and ignoring the quiet prep table. Resentment would be easy and almost pleasant. Mina hands him the serving ladle, points to the meal tickets, and gives him a visible task that also moves the line.

That is not approval. It is social intelligence. If the vain helper is still helping, she can use the help while guarding the work from vanity's damage. If he endangers the line, she corrects him. Either way, her act stays joined to the whole.

Robert feels the old insult land at the kitchen table. The estate folder is open, the photocopied will is between them, and one sibling has reached back twenty years for a sentence that still knows its way under his ribs. He leaves the insult unanswered and asks which bill must be paid before Friday.

There is no victory in becoming the exact shape of the interruption. The useful act is waiting, and anger is asking to wear your hands.

examples.title: Fiona Keeps Triage

planSpec.audience: Fiona facing a furious family member
planSpec.stakes: anger could sever her from the next correct triage act
planSpec.requiredBeat: Fiona names the wait, checks the chart, and gives the next update without matching the shout.

examples.scenario: The triage printer jams while a man pounds the counter beside a strip of waiting-room wristbands. Fiona must decide whether to answer the shout or finish the next care act. She names the delay, checks the chart screen, and gives the family the next honest update in the same low voice. The medication cart is blocking the corridor, so the next clear update matters more than winning the counter.
examples.whatToDo: Name the delay, check the chart, and give the next accurate update without matching the shout.
examples.whyItMatters: The social act is not passive. Fiona still gives information, but she refuses to let another person's volume choose her manner.

examples.title: Luca Patches First

planSpec.audience: Luca receiving a dismissive review comment
planSpec.stakes: pride could turn a fixable bug into a feud
planSpec.requiredBeat: "The bug is real even if the sentence is ugly," Luca says, then patches the null case.

examples.scenario: "Did you even test the null case?" the review thread asks above a red test output. Luca's cursor rests over a defensive reply, then moves to the fixture instead. He patches the null case, adds the failing test, and writes that the bug was valid while the tone made review harder. The failing test is still red, and the null fixture will remain broken after any clever reply.
examples.whatToDo: Patch the valid bug first, then answer the tone without turning the thread into a feud.
examples.whyItMatters: He separates the useful correction from the insult, so pride does not turn a fixable defect into a feud.

examples.title: Margaux Splits the Dispute

planSpec.audience: Margaux mediating branches over a fence
planSpec.stakes: two homeowners want victory more than shade or safety
planSpec.requiredBeat: Margaux draws the property line and the diseased limb separately before either neighbor speaks again.

examples.scenario: Sawdust dots the snow under the leaning maple before either neighbor stops talking. Margaux can let the loudest grievance set the agenda, or she can split the problem. She draws the property line from the survey, circles the diseased limb from the arborist note, and puts orange tape only where safety requires action. The saw crew is waiting by the curb, so the line between safety and pride has to be drawn now.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the property line, the diseased limb, and the pride dispute before choosing the next action.
examples.whyItMatters: Anger wants one winner. The social move distinguishes property, safety, and pride before anyone is made an enemy.

examples.title: Brennan Reviews the Stroke

planSpec.audience: Brennan coaching after a lost race
planSpec.stakes: blame would cut one athlete from the crew's common work
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Brennan replay the missed stroke, then ask each rower for the next synchronized correction.

examples.scenario: You hear eight oarlocks click out of time on the race video while Brennan stands in the erg room with the lineup card. He has to choose between naming one rower as the loss and restoring synchronized work. He replays the missed stroke, asks each rower for one correction, and writes the next drill beside each seat. The whiteboard still lists tomorrow's practice pieces, and the lineup card needs a repair plan.
examples.whatToDo: Replay the mistake, name the synchronized correction, and give every seat a next drill.
examples.whyItMatters: A postmortem can correct failure without cutting one person out of the crew's common labor.

examples.title: Mina Uses the Help

planSpec.audience: Mina working beside a volunteer who keeps grandstanding
planSpec.stakes: resentment at vanity could become another unsocial act
planSpec.requiredBeat: What if the vain helper is still helping?

examples.scenario: What if the loud helper is still moving the line? Mina watches the volunteer drift toward the donors while the hairnet box sits unopened. She must decide whether to stew over his performance or use the remaining good in it. She gives him the serving ladle, points him at meal tickets, and keeps the food line moving. The meal tickets are stacking near the warmer, so resentment has to become an assignment or get out of the line.
examples.whatToDo: Assign the vain helper a visible, useful task with clear limits instead of feeding resentment.
examples.whyItMatters: Benevolence can be practical. She corrects vanity by assigning useful work instead of making resentment her own vanity.

examples.title: Robert Leaves the Sentence

planSpec.audience: Robert hearing an old sibling insult revived
planSpec.stakes: history wants to finish the argument for him
planSpec.requiredBeat: It took Robert one breath to see that answering the insult would abandon the actual estate decision.

examples.scenario: It took Robert one breath to leave the old sentence on the table. The estate folder was open, the photocopied will was marked, and his sibling had revived the insult perfectly. He could answer history with history; instead he pointed to the unpaid tax bill and brought the meeting back to the decision. The tax bill deadline is circled in blue, and the old insult cannot pay it.
examples.whatToDo: Let the insult sit and return the meeting to the live estate decision.
examples.whyItMatters: Not every insult deserves the steering wheel. Robert keeps the shared obligation from being swallowed by an old wound.

questions.prompt: A nurse is shouted at by a patient's son while a medication chart waits for confirmation. Which response best keeps the social act intact? The medication chart is open, and the waiting room can hear both voices.
choices: Match his volume so he understands the seriousness of delaying the chart.
Name the wait, confirm the chart, and give the next true update without contempt.
Silence may avoid rewarding the interruption pattern and remove the attention that keeps it active.
questions.explanation: The second choice keeps care moving and preserves benevolence. Matching volume lets anger choose the act; ignoring him makes pride more important than the needed update.

questions.prompt: A teammate leaves a dismissive code review comment, but the reported bug is real. What should the developer do first? The pull request is blocked until the null case is handled.
choices: Reply with an equally sharp comment before touching the code.
Close the review until the teammate rewrites the sentence.
Patch the bug and answer the tone plainly if needed.
questions.explanation: The bug is the useful social work. A plain boundary about tone can follow, but retaliation would make ego the center and delay the repair.

questions.prompt: Two neighbors are furious about a maple limb over a fence. One demands apology, the other threatens court. What is the best first move? The arborist note and survey are on the hood of a parked car.
choices: Let both vent until someone is too tired to continue.
Ask who has lived there longer and give that person priority.
Separate the property line, the safety risk, and the emotional grievance.
questions.explanation: The third choice turns one angry mass into distinct decisions. Venting may heat the conflict, and seniority does not answer the arborist or survey facts.

questions.prompt: After a lost race, a rowing coach knows one athlete missed the catch. Which postmortem best fits this lesson? The video is paused in the erg room while the crew waits for the first sentence.
choices: Tell the crew the loss proves who lacks commitment.
Naming the mistake later in private may teach the correction without making the rower absorb public embarrassment.
Replay the stroke, name the correction, and assign each seat a next drill.
questions.explanation: The coach corrects the error while preserving the crew as a common body. Blame cuts one branch away; silence avoids the useful correction.

questions.prompt: A charity volunteer keeps posing for donors but is also serving meals quickly. What response shows benevolent firmness? The donor photographer is nearby, and the food line is starting to slow.
choices: Send him home because vanity cancels every useful contribution.
Praise his generosity in public so he stays motivated.
Give him a visible serving task with clear limits and keep the line moving.
questions.explanation: The third choice uses the remaining help while limiting the vanity. Dismissing him may waste service, while flattery feeds the exact disorder.

questions.prompt: During an estate meeting, a sibling revives an old insult just as the group must decide which bill gets paid first. What should the targeted person do?
choices: Return to the bill decision unless the insult affects the estate facts.
Answer the insult fully so the meeting is finally honest.
End the meeting to prove the insult was unacceptable.
questions.explanation: The first choice keeps the shared obligation from being captured by history. The insult may need attention later, but answering it now abandons the active duty.

questions.prompt: During a case where manager prides herself on staying calm, but internally she enjoys making difficult employees look foolish in meetings. What is the problem? The employees in the room can feel the difference between correction and a trap.
choices: Her calm is only performance if it serves humiliation.
She should show more visible anger so people trust her honesty.
Her inner motives are irrelevant if her voice stays even.
questions.explanation: Phocion-like mildness has to be real, not a mask for point-scoring. A quiet voice can still be unsocial if it aims at humiliation.

questions.prompt: In a situation where customer makes a false accusation in a crowded shop. The clerk can correct the record with one sentence or expose the customer's ignorance at length. Which choice fits?
choices: Use the one sentence that corrects the record and protects the work.
Humiliate the customer so no one tries it again.
Say nothing, because any correction would be anger.
questions.explanation: Correction is allowed; contempt is the extra injury. Silence is not required, but the correction should serve truth and order rather than revenge.

questions.prompt: After a scenario where friend disappoints you in a predictable way again. Which thought best applies the nine-rule spirit without excusing the behavior? The boundary still matters, but the next answer can be clear without being tyrannical.
choices: People should not repeat flaws once I have named them.
I can set the boundary while remembering that repeated human error is not a cosmic surprise.
Because mistakes are common, I should stop caring about the boundary.
questions.explanation: The second answer combines realism and action. Expecting flawed people never to err is impossible; dropping the boundary would confuse benevolence with surrender.

reviewCards.front: Someone obstructs your task and you feel contempt rising. What is the first distinction to make?
reviewCards.back: Separate the useful correction from the urge to sever the person from your concern.

reviewCards.front: A rude comment contains a real point. What should you retrieve from it?
reviewCards.back: Take the true part and address the tone without letting pride delay the repair.

reviewCards.front: Why is anger like cutting a branch from a tree?
reviewCards.back: Hatred separates you from the social whole even when someone else caused the first problem.

reviewCards.front: What marks genuine mildness, not performed niceness?

chapters.title: Book XII
chapters.hook: The notary stamp waits beside two untouched glasses, and Monica has to make the true page present.
chapters.counterintuition: Death reflection can look dark and still brighten the present enough for truth and justice to start now.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Live the present cleanly: separate impressions, practice the weak faculty, tell the truth, and let each completed act be enough.

breakdown.fastRead:
The notary stamp waits beside two untouched glasses of water. Monica can turn the medical directive into a dramatic conversation about fear, or she can read the page aloud, sign it, and ask for the next sheet. The present is the only room where justice can stand.

The closing discipline is not gloom. It is compression. Past regret, future fear, body discomfort, reputation, and other people's voices all ask to crowd the ruling faculty. The work is to separate them, look at the act in front of you, and do it plainly. Death matters because it asks whether life has begun yet.
breakdown.deepRead:
Metal filings cling to the sweat on Jonas's wrist. The rasp feels clumsy in his left hand, the hoof stand wobbles, and the leather apron catches on his knee each time he shifts. He wants to call the awkwardness proof. The trainer asks for one safer stroke, then one more, until the left hand steadies enough to hold the hoof without drama.

The left hand on the bridle proves that practice can answer despair. Many impossibilities are only untrained motions speaking loudly. A faculty that has never been used will report failure as identity. The answer is not optimism. The answer is practice under the exact condition that makes the motion feel weak.

Empedocles' sphere gives the mind an image of present wholeness without escape from action. The point is not to float above the world, untouched by forms, bodies, deadlines, or pain. The point is to stop dragging past and future through the ruling faculty until it loses its roundness. A mind can be whole while a pen moves, a tray is checked, a bag tag is traced, or a difficult truth is spoken.

Bridget hears the same airport complaint for the sixth time before lunch. Her last day is circled on the calendar, and the story of quitting wants to arrive before the passenger's bag tag. She says, "Bag tag first," opens the claim screen, and completes the trace. Then she can have whatever story is still true.

The phrase pancratiast not gladiator means the weapon is in the hand itself: readiness cannot be misplaced. A gladiator can drop the sword and be helpless. A practiced principle should live closer than that. If the rule is true, say it now. If the act is just, do it now. If the impression is noise, release it now.
breakdown.fullRead:
You see the indicator strip before you see the mistake report. Hadiya has already replayed yesterday's sterilizer error three times, and each replay makes the next tray blur. She can let self-reproach become another contaminant, or she can divide the work: instrument, wrapper, indicator, log. One clean set at a time.

Present-only living is often misunderstood as spontaneity. It is stricter than that. It asks you to stop spending the only usable hour on past defense or future theater. It asks whether this sentence is true, whether this form is just, whether this hand can practice, whether this impression has been examined, and whether the act in front of you has been completed without disguise.

What would change if this were the last clean hour of the work?

Alice finds out during the tenant repair postmortem. The ceiling stain has spread beyond the first leak photos, the inspection form is in her folder, and the landlord wants a softer phrase than uninhabitable. Peace would be easy for five minutes. Justice would be harder for the whole building. She writes the true condition, attaches the photos, and offers the legal next step.

The lamp image matters because it refuses a theatrical ending. A lamp shines until it is extinguished; it does not spend its final light announcing that light will soon be gone. Truth, justice, and temperance should work the same way. They are not decorations for favorable years. They are the splendor that should remain while there is still oil to burn.

The mariner and waveless bay image means calm is opinion released after the turn. The sea has not stopped being sea. The promontory has not vanished. The mariner has doubled it, and the same water feels different because the dangerous angle has been passed. When you cast away the opinion that the insult ruins you, the delay defines you, or the ending steals the completed act, calm appears without requiring the world to be remade.

Pierre closes the workshop after forty years. The broom scratches under the bench, the ledger book lies open, and the workbench key is heavy in his palm. Identity grief wants to say the series is damaged because it ends. He sweeps the last strip of dust, closes the ledger, and leaves the key where the next owner can find it.

A completed act is not harmed by ceasing. That sentence is hard to believe when the ending is yours, but it is the sentence that lets the present become usable. The medical directive can be signed. The weak hand can practice. The lost bag can be traced. The tray can be cleaned. The truth can be said. The shop can close.

The final discipline is plain enough to be missed: join one good act to the next without leaving theatrical gaps between them. The directive, hoof, bag tag, tray, ledger, and leak report are not symbols first. They are the places where a life either begins now or keeps waiting.

No one has to admire the departure. The question is quieter: did the divine within get to do its work before the door closed?

examples.title: Monica Signs the Page

planSpec.audience: Monica signing medical directives with her partner
planSpec.stakes: fear of death could delay the truthful present act
planSpec.requiredBeat: Monica reads the directive aloud, signs it, and asks the witness for the next page instead of changing the subject.

examples.scenario: The notary stamp waits beside two untouched glasses of water while the blue pen lies across the medical directive. Monica has to choose between making a joke about later and making the page true now. She reads the directive aloud, signs it, and asks the witness for the next page. Her partner watches the witness line, and the next page will not become easier by being avoided. The notary clears his throat once, and Monica keeps her eyes on the line she can complete.
examples.whatToDo: Read the directive, sign the true page, and move to the next required sheet without turning away.
examples.whyItMatters: Death reflection becomes useful only when it starts the present act instead of becoming a mood.

examples.title: Jonas Trains the Rasp

planSpec.audience: Jonas practicing with his weak hand
planSpec.stakes: awkwardness feels like proof he cannot learn
planSpec.requiredBeat: Jonas uses his left hand for the rasp until the motion steadies enough to hold the hoof safely.

examples.scenario: Metal filings cling to the sweat on Jonas's wrist as the rasp chatters against the hoof stand. His leather apron twists when he shifts, and he must decide whether awkward means impossible. He keeps the rasp in his left hand until the motion steadies enough to hold the hoof safely. The horse shifts once against the hoof stand, so the safer practiced stroke matters now. The trainer does not praise the stroke yet, but the hoof is safer than it was one minute earlier.
examples.whatToDo: Practice the weak motion under supervision until it becomes safe enough for the next stroke.
examples.whyItMatters: The weak faculty should be trained before it is trusted or condemned. Despair is often early evidence, not final evidence.

examples.title: Bridget Traces the Bag

planSpec.audience: Bridget handling a final flight before quitting
planSpec.stakes: past frustration and future resignation threaten the present customer
planSpec.requiredBeat: "Bag tag first," Bridget says, and completes the trace before indulging the story of how done she is.

examples.scenario: Bridget hears, "My bag was on the app ten minutes ago," as the passenger waves a boarding pass over the claim screen. Bridget's resignation letter is printed in her locker, and she can feel the quitting speech rising. She says, "Bag tag first," enters the number, and finishes the trace before touching the story of being done. The baggage belt has stopped moving, and the passenger can still be helped before the quitting story returns. The claim number appears on the screen, which gives Bridget a present fact stronger than her resignation story.
examples.whatToDo: Put the bag tag before the quitting story and complete the trace in the present customer case.
examples.whyItMatters: The final day still contains a duty. Future departure does not excuse a thin present act.

examples.title: Hadiya Cleans the Next Set

planSpec.audience: Hadiya preparing trays after an error report
planSpec.stakes: self-reproach could overpower the clean next procedure
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Hadiya divide the tray into instrument, wrapper, indicator, and log until the next set is clean.

examples.scenario: Hadiya checks the indicator strip before the mistake report clipped to the sterilizer log. Hadiya does not need another loop of self-accusation; she needs a clean tray. She divides the next set into instrument, wrapper, indicator, and log until the procedure cart is ready. The next surgery tray is due before noon, so clean sequence has to replace clean feelings. The sterilizer door is still warm, and the next tray needs sequence more than self-punishment.
examples.whatToDo: Break the next tray into inspectable parts and clean each part instead of rehearsing guilt.
examples.whyItMatters: Separating the present object restores agency. Reproach can look moral while it weakens the next procedure.

examples.title: Pierre Leaves the Key

planSpec.audience: Pierre closing his workshop after forty years
planSpec.stakes: identity grief tries to make ending look like failure
planSpec.requiredBeat: It took Pierre one final sweep to see that a completed series of work is not harmed by ending.

examples.scenario: It took Pierre one final sweep to hear the shop become quiet. The broom leaned against the workbench, the ledger book lay closed, and the key pressed into his palm. He could treat ending as failure; instead he swept the last strip of dust, locked the drawer, and left the workbench key for the next owner. The shop lights are already off in the back room, and the ledger still needs its final mark. The key ring sounds final on the bench, but the last sweep still belongs to Pierre.
examples.whatToDo: Complete the closing tasks and treat the finished series as finished, not ruined.
examples.whyItMatters: An activity that ends at its proper time is not made false by ending.

examples.title: Alice Says Uninhabitable

planSpec.audience: Alice choosing truth with an angry landlord
planSpec.stakes: a false reassurance would buy peace and lose justice
planSpec.requiredBeat: What must be said if this were the last clean hour of the work?

examples.scenario: Alice asks what word would stay true if this were the last clean hour of the work. Alice looks at the ceiling stain, the leak photos, and the inspection form while the landlord asks for softer language. She can buy peace or protect the tenant. She writes uninhabitable, documents the leak, and lists the legal next step. The tenant is waiting in the hallway, where the softer word would become an unsafe night. The inspection form will outlast the argument, so Alice chooses the word a tenant can rely on.
examples.whatToDo: Use the accurate condition word, attach the evidence, and state the legal next step.
examples.whyItMatters: The present demand for truth matters more than the temporary peace a false reassurance would buy.

questions.prompt: A patient is avoiding an end-of-life directive because signing feels gloomy. Which action best uses mortality as a present discipline? The notary has the stamp ready, and her partner is waiting beside the witness line.
choices: Read the directive aloud, sign the true page, and continue to the next required form.
Wait until the subject feels less heavy so the signature is emotionally clean.
Talk about every possible future fear before deciding whether the page is needed.
questions.explanation: The first choice lets death reflection start a truthful present act. Waiting and spiraling both give fear more authority than the page in front of her.

questions.prompt: An apprentice's weak hand makes a basic motion clumsy, and he wants to conclude he is not suited for the work. What should he do? The hoof is lifted, the rasp is in the wrong hand, and the trainer is watching for safety.
choices: Switch permanently to the strong hand so the lesson feels successful.
Practice the weak motion safely before treating awkwardness as a verdict.
Quit the task until confidence returns on its own.
questions.explanation: The left-hand image teaches practice before despair. The strong hand may hide the gap, while waiting for confidence skips the training that creates it.

questions.prompt: A lost-luggage clerk is on her final shift and feels that quitting soon makes today's complaint meaningless. What response fits present-only action? The claim screen is open, and the passenger still needs an answer from this shift.
choices: Tell the passenger she is leaving soon and cannot fix the system.
Finish the trace before indulging the story of being done.
Let a coworker handle the case because her future is elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The present customer still has a claim to Bridget's act. Her resignation is real, but using it first would let the future thin the current duty.

questions.prompt: In a situation where sterilization technician keeps replaying yesterday's error while the next instrument tray waits. Which move best separates impression from work? The next tray is due before noon, and the error report is clipped beside the log.
choices: Divide the next tray into instrument, wrapper, indicator, and log, then clean each part.
Keep reviewing the mistake until she feels punished enough to continue.
Ask someone else to finish all trays so she cannot repeat the error.
questions.explanation: The first choice turns guilt into inspectable present action. Punishment loops feel serious but do not clean the next tray; avoidance abandons the faculty that needs practice.

questions.prompt: After a scenario where craftsman closing a workshop after decades thinks the ending makes the whole career smaller. Which thought best applies the completed-act idea? The ledger is open on the bench, and the key has to be left for the next owner.
choices: Sustained commitment may appear when someone keeps engaging past normal stopping points and resists a convenient exit.
The ending proves the shop was only an identity prop.
A finished series is not damaged by finishing at its proper time.
questions.explanation: The third answer treats completion as completion, not failure. The other choices let identity grief rewrite the value of the acts already done.

questions.prompt: Before acting in a case where housing inspector can soften a report to calm an angry landlord, but the unit is unsafe. What should guide the sentence? The leak photos are timestamped, and the tenant cannot sleep under softer wording.
choices: Use the accurate condition word and attach the evidence.
Choose the wording least likely to cause conflict today.
Delay the report until the landlord is easier to persuade.
questions.explanation: Truth and justice are the live duties. Softer wording buys temporary peace by losing accuracy, and delay lets fear govern the present hour.

questions.prompt: Suppose a leader claims to value the present but spends each decision defending old choices or predicting future blame. What has gone wrong? The decision memo is due today, so old defense and future blame are both crowding the page.
choices: He has confused present action with constant reference to past and future narratives.
He is being responsible because every decision should settle all time at once.
Direct action may break the paralysis created by three earlier rounds of consequence planning.
questions.explanation: The present is not impulse; it is the only point where a just act can be made. Past defense and future blame are impressions crowding the faculty.

questions.prompt: Someone says, "I will tell the truth after I get through this uncomfortable week." Which reply best captures the lamp image? The uncomfortable week is already here, and the statement will either shine or go dark.
choices: Truth can wait because timing matters more than character.
A lamp should shine while it has oil; truth should not go dark before the end.
Silence may seem neutral because the team is overloaded and a true observation could land as criticism.
questions.explanation: The lamp keeps shining until it is extinguished. Delaying truth because the week is uncomfortable makes convenience, not character, set the limit.

questions.prompt: Two details frame the case: a team is consumed by the opinion that one setback ruins the whole project. Which evaluation best applies the waveless-bay image? The project board is still usable if the team drops the ruin story before planning.
choices: The setback must disappear before the team can regain calm.
The team should pretend the setback is positive so morale survives.
The team can release the ruin story, inspect the facts, and find the next stable action.
questions.explanation: The bay appears when opinion is released, not when the world becomes easy. Pretending positivity is another opinion; factual inspection restores action.

reviewCards.back: Cast away the ruin opinion, inspect what remains, and take the next stable action.
